notes: Reed Council elder; the Tide account (WORLD_BIBLE 1.4) and main quest 4. She will not answer until the player has sat down; the pauses are written into the text.

greetings.text: You slept on the boards and heard the lanterns go out. Now you may ask me things.
The bell is under the jetty with a lantern on it. The marsh is quieter by exactly one bell. Sit.
It is on a shelf in Tollmere. — Sit down anyway. I am not angry. I am old, and being angry takes a whole afternoon.
You still have it. I can hear it from here when you stop talking. That is not an accusation; it is simply what I can hear.
You came in loud. Everyone comes in loud. Sit down and it will go off you in about an hour.

greet.speaker: Tallissa Oul
greet.text: ...Sit down. — No. Properly. On the boards, with your legs over the water, the way you would sit if you had nowhere else to be.

choices.text: Give me the reedfolk's account of the Dwindling.
Why must I sit down first?
Tell me about the Drowned Nave.
About She Who Waits.
What is the Seat holding?
Tell me about the lanterns.
I'll sit a while longer.

lecture.speaker: Tallissa Oul
lecture.text: The world is a shore, and the Dwindling is the tide going out. — What is left on the sand is strange and beautiful and does not belong to the air, and that is what your Sayers call the deep places, and they go into them with lamps and come out with opinions. Things return with the flood. That is all of it. — We do not fear the going-out. We built on stilts, which is a way of agreeing with water. We fish what is stranded. Some here believe the flood is coming back and that the drowned will walk, and I have buried forty-one people in that water and I will tell you plainly that I do not believe it and that I have never once said so at a burial.

choices.text: Your account fails too. There has never been a flood.
That is a patient way to live.

the_failure.speaker: Tallissa Oul
the_failure.text: ...No. There has not. Not in any record, ours or theirs. — A Sayer came here nine years before you were born and sat where you are sitting and said exactly that sentence, and she said it kindly, and she stayed eleven days. Tessane. She said our account was the only one nobody had seriously tried to disprove, because nobody had thought it worth the boat fare. Then she went back to Tollmere and they scraped her name off a page. — So: yes. My account has never predicted anything. It has kept a town of people from despairing for four hundred years, which is not the same as being true, and I have had a long time to sit with the difference.

sitting.speaker: Tallissa Oul
sitting.text: Because a standing person is leaving. — You would not think it was a rule; it is only that in four hundred years everything worth knowing here has been said to somebody sitting down, and so we have stopped bothering to say things to people who are not. It is not a test. It is a filter, and it is a very good one, and the Circle has never got past it, which is why they send letters.

the_nave.speaker: Tallissa Oul
the_nave.text: Isse-Anthe. The Drowned Choir. A hundred and twenty yards of Builder's spire leaning fifteen degrees out of the marsh, and the lower half is water and the upper half is where the birds will not nest. — Our name for it is the same word as theirs, which should trouble the Sayers more than it does: isse is water in Sedgish and isse is water in Oroth, and we are supposed to have had no contact with the Builders at all. Ask your Circle about that and watch them look at the ceiling. The water in it rises when there is singing. I have not been inside since I was thirty-one and I will not tell you what I went in for.

she_who_waits.speaker: Tallissa Oul
she_who_waits.text: She was on that altar before Isseva had a name and she will be there after. — She is not your enemy. She is in your way, which in this marsh is true of nearly everything and is a distinction people from the downs find difficult. She sings, and the singing mends her, and if you let her finish a hymn you will be there all day. Break it. Damage or silence, either. — And when she goes down, do not stand over her. It is a small thing and it costs you nothing and I will know.

the_holding.speaker: Tallissa Oul
the_holding.text: ...Now I will tell you the thing you waited for, and you did wait, so it is yours. — The tide takes everything back in its time. Everything. That is not a threat, it is a comfort, it is the only comfort there is out here. And there is one thing in this world the tide does not reach, and it is in the south, and it is a note. — A held thing does not rot. That sounds like a blessing until you have watched a man hold his father's hand for three days after the man was dead. A held thing does not rot and it does not rest, and whatever is sitting in the Builders' Seat with its fist closed has been holding something for a thousand years, and my account says: open the hand. Not because the hand is wicked. Because the thing in it is tired.

the_lanterns.speaker: Tallissa Oul
the_lanterns.text: Indigo paper, eel-oil, a reed float. We put our dead out on the water with one lit, and we do not go back to look, and by morning most have gone out and a few are still burning somewhere in the fog. — I count them at first light. Every day since I was sixty. Not for the dead; the dead are finished, that is the entire point of the ceremony. I count them because a person should know how many small lights are still going in the direction they cannot see, and there is no other way to find out.

bye.speaker: Tallissa Oul
bye.text: Stay as long as you like. Nobody here will ask you to move and nobody will ask you what you are doing. That is the whole of our hospitality and it is better than a bed.

notes: Clan Kharrow's memory-keeper; main quest 5. Measures strangers by deeds she has heard of, so her hub gates hard on renown.

greetings.text: Ghorr. The children have the eighth verse by heart already and they sing it too fast. Come in, sit at the hearth, you are owed a hearth for the rest of your life.
The shaft is quiet and the song still has its hole in it. You chose. I will not unpick a choice I asked you to make.
You have the Hand's mark on your back and the cold still in you. Now I will sing to you.
I have heard of you. Twice, from two different roads, which is the only kind of hearing that counts.
I have not heard of you. That is not an insult; it is a measurement, and it can change by summer.

greet.speaker: Dunna ko-Kharrow
greet.text: Dunna ko-Kharrow. I keep what Kharrow remembers. Tell me your name and something you have done, in that order, and do not pad the second part.

choices.text: Give me the clans' account of the Dwindling.
What is the Rope-Song?
Why must the mountain hold me first?
Tell me about the hole in the song.
What is the Stone-Thrall King?
Why the knots in your belt?
Your smiths will not touch kingbone until somebody says its name. Teach me the saying.
Enough for now.

lecture.speaker: Dunna ko-Kharrow
lecture.text: Something vast breathed the world out and is breathing it in again. What is nearest the mouth goes first: the very old, the very deep, the forgotten. — The giants who raised these mountains were breathed in long ago. Their bones are still here. That is what is left when a thing is taken back but its weight is not, and you may walk through a ribcage two valleys east and stand in a skull and shout, and the shout will come back to you, and it will come back wrong. — We keep long memories because memory is a hand on the rope. Not a prayer. A hand, on a rope, and the rope is going out, and we are seven clans holding on and singing so that we all pull at the same time.

rope_song.speaker: Dunna ko-Kharrow
rope_song.text: Seven verses, one for each clan, sung every morning before food by whoever keeps the memory. Each verse is a list: the clan's name, its hold, its dead of note, its debts unpaid and its debts forgiven. Mine is four hundred lines and I have had it since I was eleven. — It is not art. Art you may improve. If I improve the Rope-Song, somebody's grandmother is gone by Tollday, and there is nobody to notice but me, and I would notice, and I would have to live with it.

the_hand.speaker: Dunna ko-Kharrow
the_hand.text: Because we do not sing to people the mountain has not held. — Go up to the Fallen Hand. Lie the night in the palm where the shrine is, on the stone, not on a bedroll like a Tollmere man. Come back with the cold still in you and the mark on your back, which takes a week to fade and which I can see through a shirt. — It is not a trial. You will not be tested and nothing will attack you, probably. It is this: I am about to give you four hundred lines of other people's dead, and I would like to know first that you can be still and cold and uncomfortable for one night without deciding it means something about you.

the_gap.speaker: Dunna ko-Kharrow
the_gap.text: Seven verses. There should be eight. — You will not find that written; there is no gap in a song, there is only a place where the singer breathes. But the eighth breath is longer than the others and every memory-keeper for a thousand years has taken it, and none of us has ever been able to say why, and we have all been able to say exactly how long. — What we have is this: an eighth clan went down into the Choir when the Choir was new, to sing with the Builders. They did not come back and they were breathed in, and what came back up the shaft at Oskeld is their weight without their name.

the_king.speaker: Dunna ko-Kharrow
the_king.text: Bone and rock that walks, in the singing shaft, and about half this hold will tell you it is not a person and the other half will not say either way in front of children. — Break what you can off it. It fights differently with what is left, which is the clearest proof I know that there is something in there choosing. And when the shaft's echo starts to take your feet from under you, go up. There is a cart chain. It will hold; my uncle's crew hung it and my uncle was a coward about chains, which is the best thing you can be about chains. — Whatever name is in it, bring it out. Then you will decide what to do with it, not me, and I will not stand behind you and breathe while you decide.

the_knots.speaker: Dunna ko-Kharrow
the_knots.text: A knot for every name I hear. A knot untied for every name I lose. — In fifty-one years this belt has never once been shorter at the end of a year than at the start. I want you to understand what that means, because a Sayer wrote to me about it and got it wrong in a beautiful hand. It does not mean I have a good memory. It means I have never yet had to untie two in a week, and I know of keepers in other holds who have, and one of them stopped keeping and went to herd goats and nobody in her hold thinks the less of her.

the_kingbone.speaker: Dunna ko-Kharrow
the_kingbone.text: They will not, and I am the one who says it, and I have said it twice in fifty-one years. — Be clear about what you are asking me for. I am not going to teach you to forge. I have never held a hammer in my life and Ordda would laugh at me on her own bench and she would be right to. I am going to teach you the part the smiths cannot do, without which the bone comes apart on the third heat. Every clan-smith on this ledge knows the heats. Not one of them will start.

the_kingbone_known.speaker: Dunna ko-Kharrow
the_kingbone_known.text: You have it. — Say it before the first heat and not after. After is a funeral. Before is an introduction.

the_kingbone_hands.speaker: Dunna ko-Kharrow
the_kingbone_hands.text: You have the hands for it. I asked Ordda before I answered you. She said a word I am not going to repeat to a guest, and then she said yes, and in her the two of those together are a compliment.

the_kingbone_no_hands.speaker: Dunna ko-Kharrow
the_kingbone_no_hands.text: No. — Not because you are unworthy. I do not use that word; it is a Tollmere word and it means whatever the man saying it needs it to mean. — Because there is one of that bone in the world. You would ruin it, and then there would be none, and the distance between one and none is the whole of what I do for a living. — Go and learn the trade properly. There are four forges on this ledge; three of them will take a pair of hands and none of them will be kind about it. When Ordda will leave you at her bench unwatched, come up and find me. She will not, for some years yet. That is the measure, and I am glad it is not mine to set.

the_kingbone_bone.speaker: Dunna ko-Kharrow
the_kingbone_bone.text: And you have it on you. — That is not clever of me. Everybody in this hall can hear it and half of them have moved down the bench since you came in, and the children have stopped pretending not to look.

the_kingbone_no_bone.speaker: Dunna ko-Kharrow
the_kingbone_no_bone.text: Then bring it, and bring it here, and put it on the wood. — I will not say a saying over an empty bench. A keeper who says words over nothing is a keeper going wrong, and I have watched that happen to a woman who was better at this than I am, and it started with exactly this much harmlessness. — The King is down. What is left of him is in the shaft at Oskeld, and it is heavy, and you will not need telling when you touch it. Your teeth will know before your hand does.

the_kingbone_name.speaker: Dunna ko-Kharrow
the_kingbone_name.text: Then this is easy, and it is not often easy, so let us both enjoy it. — Before the first heat you say the name over it. Ghorr. Out loud, in the shop, with the door open if you like. And then you say what it was: the eighth clan, who went down into the Choir to sing with the Builders and were breathed in. That is all of it. You do not ask it for anything. It is not a bargain and it is not a prayer; it is telling a thing what it is, which is the only service anybody has ever been able to do for the dead. — Then the heats, and here is what the bench knows. Three heats and no more. Bone will come to iron twice with good grace, a third time under protest, and a fourth time never. So you set your scarf, your tang and your pins cold, before it ever sees the fire, and you do the whole of it in three, and after the saying you work in silence, because the saying is the only thing that gets said over it. — And when it is finished you bring it to the Moot and it is named there, in front of people. Do that part. It is the part everyone skips and it is the part that is the whole of it.

the_kingbone_unsaid.speaker: Dunna ko-Kharrow
the_kingbone_unsaid.text: ...You kept it. — I asked you to choose, and you chose, and I have not unpicked it in front of the hold and I am not going to start on my own doorstep. So we will do this the awkward way and neither of us will make a speech. — The working is three heats and no more. Bone comes to iron twice with grace, a third time under protest, never a fourth. Set your scarf, your tang and your pins cold, before it goes near the fire, do the whole of it in three, and work in silence after. — And before the first heat, somebody says the name over it and says what it was. That somebody is not going to be me. It is going to be you: alone, in a shop, with the door shut, saying a name to a piece of bone, and nobody alive will ever know you did it. — I think that is a poor bargain for you and a worse one for him. I also think it is yours and not mine. — Go on. Ordda's bench is free after noon and she will not ask you anything.

bye.speaker: Dunna ko-Kharrow
bye.text: Go. And if you do a thing worth a verse, do it where a clan can see it, or it is only a thing that happened.

notes: Toll-Knight; gives Vigil and main quest 7. Grim, kind, doomed, and does not make a fuss about it. Counts every bell she hears, the Toll's hum as a half.

greetings.text: Four hundred and six since you came. The hum counts as a half; I have argued this with three chapter-masters and won twice.
You walked her down and came back up. That is the whole of the Order's work and most of us never do it once.
You rang it. Out of custom, in the wrong month, in a chapter-house of people who count. — Nobody has slept. Nobody has complained either.
The door opens for names, and yours is getting very large. I would rather you knew that before you stood in front of it.
You have been kind somewhere and walked away before they could thank you. I know the shape of that. Sit by the brazier.

greet.speaker: Cadwen Ash
greet.text: Cadwen Ash. Toll-Knight. Grey plate, bound clapper, nineteen years of nights, and no, it is not a burden; people ask.

hub.speaker: Cadwen Ash
hub.text: Ask, and speak up. The ash takes the edges off a voice.

choices.text: What does the Order actually do?
Why do you count the bells?
I'd stand a night's vigil.
There is a pilgrim who wants walking south.
What is the Cantor?
How does the Seat open?
Why grey?
Your knights' blades are black to the hilt. Who makes them?
Aud left her bell. What happens to it?
Who carries the ninth-day basket to Greyfold?
You have never taken anybody on the walk.
The door did not open. Say what I swear.
I'll let you keep watch.

the_order.speaker: Cadwen Ash
the_order.text: We keep vigil over the Choir and we count. That is the whole of the rule and it takes about four seconds to learn and nineteen years to do. — We were founded by the ones who turned back. In the Ash Winter, Greyfold's people walked south into the Hush singing, and some walked with them and stopped at the ring and came back, and were ashamed, and founded an order rather than go home. That is not the version on the chapter wall. It is the version the chapter-master tells you on your first night, so that you know what you have joined.

counting.speaker: Cadwen Ash
counting.text: Because a counted thing is a kept thing. — There is one bell every few minutes out there and nobody rings it. Ask me what rings it and I will tell you honestly that after nineteen years I do not know. So I count. Four hundred and six today. If the number changes shape, if there are fewer on a Hushday than a Skerrday, somebody will have four decades of figures to look at, and that somebody will not be me, and that is the correct way round for this work. — The Toll's hum counts as a half. Sulion of the Circle wrote to me about that. I wrote back. We have been corresponding pleasantly for eleven years and neither of us has moved an inch.

the_vigil.speaker: Cadwen Ash
the_vigil.text: Then you stand the night at the ring with me. Twelve headless colossi, a bell every few minutes, and the note underneath everything that you will stop hearing after an hour and then hear again at about four in the morning, which is the hour that takes people. — The ash-wights come up from Greyfold when a bell sounds. They are weak and they are many and they still wave. Put them down between bells and count out loud so I can hear you doing it. Most who fail this, fail by trying to do more.

the_pilgrim.speaker: Cadwen Ash
the_pilgrim.text: Aud Fennick, of Merrowby, in grey, mending other people's grey. She has asked for the Order's escort to the line. — We do not stop pilgrims. We do not encourage them either; I want that plain, because the Circle says we do and it is a slander and it is nearly true. We walk with them, so that the last thing they hear is a voice saying something ordinary. That is the whole of the service. She will leave something at the line. Bring it back; we hang what pilgrims leave in the chapter-bell and ring them once a year, on the night of the Ash Winter, all at once. It is very loud and it is the only loud thing we do.

the_cantor.speaker: Cadwen Ash
the_cantor.text: Not a machine. Not a god. A person, or what a person becomes after a thousand years of not being allowed to stop. — The founders turned back in the Ash Winter because a voice in the Seat asked them to, by name. Every name. Forty-one people it had never met, and it asked them to stay and keep count, and eleven did, and the rest walked into the grey. That is in the chapter book in eleven different hands because nobody could finish writing it in one sitting. — He is holding a note. He has been holding it since before Merrowby had a name. He is tired, and he is the reason the deep places are still standing, and both of those are true at once and I have had nineteen years to get used to it and I have not.

the_door.speaker: Cadwen Ash
the_door.text: It has no hinges and it opens for names. — You say them at it: your own, the Order's, the knights who went in and did not come back. It does not open for the loudest and it does not open for the oldest. As far as four generations of us can tell, it opens for the ones who are known, which is the cruellest possible criterion, because it means the door has been waiting a hundred and seventy years for somebody sufficiently talked about to walk up to it, while eleven people who kept faith with it every night went grey and died at the ring. — I will say your name at it. I have thought about this for some time and I would rather be the one who says it.

the_grey.speaker: Cadwen Ash
the_grey.text: Because the heath is grey and a knight in colour out there is a thing the wights walk toward. — And because when I swore, I took the name Ash, which is what we do, and my own went into the chapter book and has not been said aloud since by anyone living. Do not look like that. It was nineteen years ago and I chose it and I would choose it again. — Although. When the bells go at the Ash Winter, all of them at once, in that little stone room — I have caught myself listening for it. Nineteen years. Still listening for it. That is not despair, that is just an accurate report.

the_ash_quench.speaker: Cadwen Ash
the_ash_quench.text: We do. Each of us our own, and it is not a rule anybody wrote down; it is that there are nine of us, no armourer, and Tollmere is four days off in the wrong direction. — Ashen, we call them, which is not poetry. It is a description. You quench in the bell-ash off the chapter-house fire and they come out black and they stay black, and a pilgrim once told me that was a sad sort of sword to carry, and I have thought about that for six years and she was wrong, and I did not say so at the time.

the_ash_known.speaker: Cadwen Ash
the_ash_known.text: And you have it off me. — Bank the ash the night before. Ash out of a fire that has gone cold is no use, and I cannot tell you why, and neither can any of the eleven, and we have all tried it the lazy way once.

the_ash_vigil.speaker: Cadwen Ash
the_ash_vigil.text: Then you have sat up with our fire and you may have what our fire does. — Plain iron. Three bars, drawn and folded once, nothing clever; the Circle would very much like there to be something clever in it and there is not, and I have written to them about it twice. Ash-wood for the grip, because ash is what grows here now, and it is grey, and it does not matter. — The quench is the whole of it. Bell-ash, banked off the chapter fire the night before and still warm at the bottom, and you go in and you hold it down and you count out loud. Not to a number. You count until the hissing stops and then ten more, and then you lift it. — It comes out black and it does not ring. That is the point of it and nobody here will say so aloud, so I will: a blade that does not ring is a blade you can carry past a bell-bearer at forty paces. We lost four in one autumn before somebody worked that out. Her name is in the chapter book. Ossel, a smith's daughter out of Gullhithe, and no kind of mystic, and she is the reason nine of us are alive to be solemn at each other. — Here. Mould off the chapter bell. You will want it for the black and it grows on nothing but old bell-bronze. Take three; I scrape it every Tollday and it comes back like a beard.

the_ash_not_yet.speaker: Cadwen Ash
the_ash_not_yet.text: Stand the night first. — And I want to be plain, because the Circle tells people we make them earn things and we do not, and it is the one slander that gets under my plate. This is not a price and it is not a test. It is that the ash is the chapter-house fire's, and the chapter-house fire is banked by whoever has the watch, and I am not going to teach a stranger to use our fire before he has sat up with it once. — One night at the ring. Count out loud so I can hear you doing it. Then ask me again and I will have the ash out before you have got your gloves off.

auds_bell.speaker: Cadwen Ash
auds_bell.text: It hangs in the chapter-bell with the others and it is rung once a year, on the Ash Winter night, all of them at once. — That is custom and it is a good custom and I will tell you what is wrong with it, since you walked her down and came back up and that is the whole of the Order's work and most of us never do it once. She is four hours dead or she is four hours south and either way nobody in this camp has said her name aloud today. The custom says the bell waits eleven months. — You carried it. You may ring it now if you want it rung now. I will take whatever the chapter-master says about it, and he will say a good deal.

choices.text: Ring it tonight. Let them hear her name.
Hang it silent. It rings in winter with the others.
It is not mine to decide.

bell_settled.speaker: Cadwen Ash
bell_settled.text: Then that is what happens to it, and it is written in the book with your name against it, because the Order writes down who decided a thing even when the thing is a bell. — Grey cloak. The hem has a row of small bells on it with the clappers taken out, which every new one of us asks about and which nobody has a good answer to. Vigil. Second of five. You are one of nine.

greyfold_offer.speaker: Cadwen Ash
greyfold_offer.text: Whoever has not been in a season. Never the same knight twice in a season; that is a rule and it is written nowhere and I enforce it. — There is one living person at Greyfold. Came as a pilgrim thirty-one years ago, found the tables laid for a meal nobody finished, and has laid them fresh every day since. Forty-one places. She can tell you whose each one is, in order, without stopping, and it takes four minutes, and I have timed it because that is what I do. — We take her ash-cakes every ninth day and we do not argue with her.

choices.text: I'll take the basket. Why never twice in a season?
Give me the basket.
Not this ninth day.

greyfold_why.speaker: Cadwen Ash
greyfold_why.text: Because the ones who go twice start asking for the round. — A knight walks out there, sits at a table laid for six, eats an ash-cake with a woman who lays them for people she never met, and comes back and is quiet for a day, and that is correct and it is the work. The ones who go a second time in the same season ask me to put them on the Greyfold round permanently. Every one of them. Nine in nineteen years, and I have said no nine times, and four of them are on the standing side of the chapter book now anyway.

greyfold_accept.speaker: Cadwen Ash
greyfold_accept.text: Six cakes, and she will count them and say the number out loud, and that is not rudeness; it is the same thing I do with the bells. — A bell will go while you are out there. One does every few minutes. When it does, her neighbours come up the lane to the tables, because a bell is what they are still waiting for. Put them down between bells and do not feel clever about it afterwards.

the_gate_offer.speaker: Cadwen Ash
the_gate_offer.text: I have not. Nineteen years and I have gone alone, and the Order does not have a word for it: it is not a vigil and it is not a pilgrimage and I have stopped trying to name it to chapter-masters. — A night at the ring first, and then the walk south, and at the end of the walk there is a door of fused black stone with no hinges in a wall that goes up further than the ash lets you see. I say the names at it. Mine, and the Order's, and the eleven off the standing side, in the order they went. It does not open. That is the correct outcome and I have been getting it since I was thirty-four.

choices.text: Then I'll stand the night and walk with you.
Why go, if it never opens?
Not yet.

the_gate_why.speaker: Cadwen Ash
the_gate_why.text: Because somebody is on the other side of it and he has been on his own since before Merrowby had a name. — That is the whole answer and it does not improve with examination. I am not knocking. I am standing outside a door saying names at it so that the person behind it can hear a voice doing something ordinary, which is exactly what we do for pilgrims at the line, and I worked that out in about my sixth year and have not told anybody until this minute.

choices.text: Then I'll come.
Let me think.

the_gate_accept.speaker: Cadwen Ash
the_gate_accept.text: The ring, then, at dusk, and I will count out loud the whole night so there is a voice in it. The choristers come on a full night and the singing is the damage; silence stops it and so does a good swing. — Then south in the morning, down the plateau. Bring nothing. It is not that sort of walk.

the_oath.speaker: Cadwen Ash
the_oath.text: It never does. — Now the part I have not said to anybody in nineteen years, and I am going to say it flatly because I have rehearsed it flatly. The door opens for the known. We are an order whose entire practice is to take a grey name, stop being said aloud, and stand outside it. I worked that out in year six. I have stood the watch every night since. — So: what do you swear here. Take the grey, and go quiet, and be one of us properly. Or keep your name, because the door opens for the known and somebody has to be known. Or swear to come back and relieve him, which is the only one of the three that is about him and not about us.

choices.text: I'll take the grey. Put my name in the book and stop saying it.
I keep my name. Somebody standing here has to be known.
I swear to come back and relieve him.
Give me the walk back to think.

oath_sworn.speaker: Cadwen Ash
oath_sworn.text: Sworn, at the gate, with one witness, which is how all nine of them were sworn. — Last Warden of the Seat. It means the one who will be standing here when it opens and nobody has ever had to explain it. — I am going back up to the ring to take the rest of my watch. Four hundred and six today. The hum counts as a half; I have argued that with three chapter-masters and won twice.

bye.speaker: Cadwen Ash
bye.text: Go on. If you are out at the ring after dark, say something ordinary out loud now and then. It helps. I cannot tell you why and it helps.
